# Garry Kasparov: Summary
Garry Kasparov is a Russian chess grandmaster born in Baku in 1963 to a Jewish father and Armenian mother; after his father's death, he adopted his mother's surname. He began studying chess at age seven, attended Botvinnik's chess school, and became Soviet Junior Champion at thirteen. Kasparov quickly rose through the ranks, winning the World Junior Chess Championship in 1980 and becoming the youngest grandmaster at that time. He qualified for the Candidates Tournament at 19 and earned the world number one ranking in 1984, a record that lasted until 1996.
Kasparov became the youngest ever World Chess Champion in 1985 by defeating Anatoly Karpov, beginning a celebrated rivalry marked by five world title matches. His aggressive, tactical, and deeply prepared playing style, inspired by Alekhine, Tal, and Fischer, is widely considered among the greatest in history, with contributions to opening theory such as reviving the Scotch Game and innovations in the Sicilian. Kasparov broke away from FIDE in 1993, forming the PCA, and retained the classical title until his defeat by Vladimir Kramnik in 2000. He retired from regular competition in 2005 while still ranked No. 1, subsequently engaging in exhibition matches, coaching rising stars like Magnus Carlsen, playing against top-level chess computers, and founding educational and chess initiatives such as Kasparov Chess. With records for tournament victories, Olympiad medals, and holding the No. 1 spot for twenty-one years, Kasparov's legacy as a player and chess thinker remains singular, and he is broadly considered one of the greatest chess players of all time.
